title: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
summary: Ole Bielfeldt of Germany captured a microscopic view of an inkjet printer depositing ink onto paper.

summary_3_lines: 독일의 올레 빌펠트(Ole Bielfeldt)가 잉크젯 프린터 노즐에서 종이로 분사되는 미세 잉크 방울의 순간을 고해상도 현미경으로 촬영해 대상을 수상함.
일상적인 인쇄 공정 이면에서 벌어지는 초미세 유체역학 현상을 광학 기술과 시각 예술의 결합으로 구현함.
니콘 스몰월드 공모전은 전 세계 연구자와 사진가들이 참여해 미세 세계의 과학적 가치와 미학을 공유하는 장으로 자리잡음.
business_insight: 초정밀 광학 이미징 기술은 산업용 잉크젯 프린팅 및 마이크로플루이딕스(미세유체역학) 반도체 공정에서 정밀한 품질 관리와 수율 개선을 이끄는 핵심 기반 기술로 평가받고 있습니다.

title: Hackers got a four-day head start on epic PHP2Shell vulnerability
summary: Hackers were already probing the bug before defenders were told it existed.
korean_title: 보안 조직보다 4일 빨랐다… 'PHP2Shell' 제로데이 취약점 선제 악용 비상
summary_3_lines: 보안 담당자들에게 공식 경보와 패치가 전달되기 최소 4일 전부터 해커들이 'PHP2Shell' 취약점을 악용해 서버 탐색 공격을 진행함.
방어 체계가 위협의 실체를 인지하기도 전에 실제 공격 벡터가 먼저 가동된 전형적인 선행 공격 사례임.
광범위하게 사용되는 PHP 웹 환경의 특성상 취약점 노출 즉시 대규모 웹 서버 침해 및 원격 코드 실행(RCE) 위험이 가중됨.
business_insight: 제로데이 취약점 발견과 악용 간의 시간차가 사실상 역전되고 있어, 사후 패치 중심 대응을 넘어 런타임 애플리케이션 자가 보호(RASP) 및 엄격한 최소 권한 정책 등 선제적 보안 체계 구축이 시급합니다.

초당적 지지를 노렸던 급진적 식품 첨가물 규제 및 가공식품 정책 드라이브가 출범 초기부터 동력을 상실할 위기에 직면함.
business_insight: 미국 규제 당국(FDA·USDA)의 식품 안전 가이드라인 개편이 정치적 불확실성에 직면함에 따라, 글로벌 식음료 및 농축산 기업들은 단기적 정책 리스크와 장기적 규제 컴플라이언스 비용을 재점검해야 합니다.

title: Electric or gas? BMW goes both ways with new 2027 X5 and iX5.

전기차 버전인 iX5는 최대 460kW 초고속 충전 성능과 450마일(약 724km)의 긴 주행거리를 갖춰 상품성을 대폭 강화함.

business_insight: 글로벌 완성차 시장의 EV 캐즘(일시적 수요 둔화) 속에서 단일 파워트레인 올인보다 유연한 혼류 생산 전략과 획기적인 충전 스펙을 결합한 프리미엄 라인업이 가장 현실적인 수익성 방어 카드로 부상하고 있습니다.

title: Salesforce Customers Brace For New Fees to Use Claude in Its Apps
summary: Salesforce is leading the software industry’s attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps. As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce’s built-in AI products. The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms’ apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates—which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents—and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. The vast majority of workers haven’t yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps’ built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money. For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers’ AI agents haven’t started charging the tolls. They’re letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.) Starting around November, according to the company’s website , Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable “interaction,” according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently. Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn’t clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person’s computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.) Salesforce hasn’t announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce’s own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they’re reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce’s apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said. New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won’t affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. In addition to the billable “interactions,” customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a “headless license,” a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce’s new connectors until pricing is disclosed. So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce’s built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce’s customer relationship management software, Lumen made a “major” investment in using Salesforce’s AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen’s human salespeople considerable time, he said. So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been “super flexible” about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents. Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives. title: The Closing of the ‘Defenders Window’ Is Nigh
summary: At first, the X headlines this morning about the latest AI-powered cybersecurity incident seemed dire. But by the time I had a cup of coffee and began parsing all the cyber jargon, I was reassured that an apparent solution was on its way to plug a major new security hole that could make websites vulnerable to cyberintrusions. Since August, a coalition led by OpenAI has been working to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language that undergirds the web. But there was bad news, too: This type of long-simmering response to the latest AI-discovered vulnerabilities may not be viable for much longer. For months, OpenAI has been harping on what it calls the “ defender’s window ”—the critical period of time when cybersecurity experts, armed with advanced AI models, can identify and patch vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them first. The issue is that the gap is rapidly narrowing between cybercapable models from leading U.S. frontier labs and Chinese open-source models, which lack the restrictions U.S. labs impose on their models’ capabilities. Anthropic said as much in a blog post from late September warning that Chinese lab Z.ai ’s GLM-5.3 model only lags the U.S. frontier models by about four months. The good news: The Trump administration has a shiny new organization created for moments just like these. It’s called the Super Intelligence Force, a name that may elicit eyerolls from some of our more jaded readers. Still, I have heard over and over that all the AI industry wants is coordination and clarity from the White House. That, presumably, is what the SI Force will offer, led by heavy hitters including National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and senior Defense Department official Emil Michael . An OpenAI spokesperson told me today that they had briefed several agencies, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, about the PHP vulnerability, as well as briefing Clayton and Michael late last week, representing the first “major engagement” between OpenAI and the SI Force. The spokesperson added that the SI Force provided a central point to coordinate their communication across the broader government. According to a White House official, the SI Force’s work involved helping to put pressure on the “relevant parties” to deploy a vulnerability patch. While the SI Force’s coordination function may not seem terribly ambitious, at least it’s a start. It’s worth remembering that the White House essentially had to reorient its entire AI policy in April with the announcement of Mythos. The arrival of Chinese cybercapable open models could represent a Mythos 2.0 moment. I spoke with one former White House official who told me solutions from even a few months ago, like the July Gold Eagle clearinghouse that allows organizations and government agencies to share and fix software vulnerabilities, might already be outdated. It’s up to the SI Force to create a path forward. The next major internet bug likely won’t have the luxury of a two-month-long defender’s window. Meta’s Performance On Sunday, in a preview of this week’s Meta Platforms earnings report, your regular Briefing columnist, Martin Peers, declared: “If Meta can stay on investors’ good sides, an equity offering seems in the cards.” Martin nailed it on both accounts. On Wednesday afternoon, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg delivered a bunch of (mostly) good news that had investors in the company purring like kittens. Meta also announced the creation of a new category of common stock that will allow it to raise capital to fund its hefty AI investments without sacrificing Zuckerberg’s control. The highlights: For the third quarter, its revenue grew 26% to $64.6 billion, slightly above what the company had forecast. It’s trimming the losses from its Reality Labs unit. While it showed negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion rather than the positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion in the year-earlier period, that was due to its AI investments, and the number wasn’t as bad as some analysts had expected. The company’s anticipated capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for the full year, while eye-popping, were still within the range it had previously forecast. That was reassuring for investors who’ve gotten spooked in the past by sudden leaps in tech company spending on AI. Perhaps equally comforting were Zuckerberg’s reassurances that investors will see a payoff from some of its most expensive AI initiatives. He described Muse, Meta’s new agent app, as a bona fide hit for the company, one that has gained 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada in its first six weeks on the market—a faster pace of growth than for its Threads app. While Zuckerberg said the product will remain free for most people, he described a number of ways Meta plans to eventually get paid for it, including commerce transaction fees paid by businesses and money power users will pay for access to advanced models and extra tokens. Meta shares rose 2% in after-hours trading. Meta also warned of some potentially expensive new legal costs on the horizon, including from lawsuits related to child safety legal cases. During the third quarter, Meta said, its operating income declined 37% from a year earlier to just under $13 billion, due in large part to a nearly $10 billion charge related to legal proceedings. In August, the company settled a child online safety case with 52 attorneys general for $18.59 billion. And on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Meta did not say when it plans to raise capital through a new equity offering, or how much it might raise. Presumably, that will happen after Jan. 19, the effective date for issuance of the new nonvoting Class C common stock the company announced today. The company’s existing shareholders will receive a dividend of one Class C share for each share of Class A or B common stock they hold. And crucially, when the company raises money in the future with its Class C stock, that won’t dilute Zuckerberg’s voting power. “The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said. —Nick Wingfield Tongue-Tied at Tesla On Tesla’s earnings call, Elon Musk had much less to say on the topic of a potential merger of the EV maker with his other company, SpaceX, than he did Tuesday afternoon on SpaceX’s earnings call. He told investors he had said everything he wanted to on the topic for now. Tesla’s automotive revenues fell 3% to $20.56 billion while its total revenues remained flat at $28 billion compared to a year earlier. Tesla shares fell 3% in after-hours trading. —Nick Wingfield In Other News Electronic Arts plans to shed around 400 jobs, or about 3% of its staff, and shut down its BioWare studio, Bloomberg reported . Microsoft asked shareholders to approve a plan to lower CEO Satya Nadella’s pay by 6% due to falling revenue in its Xbox unit. The company also nominated Stripe co-founder John Collison to its board. Google will stop requiring local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements when it plans to build data centers in their areas. title: Datadog Offered $4 Billion to Buy Cloud Security Startup ‘Upwind’
summary: Enterprise software firm Datadog recently offered to buy Israeli cloud cybersecurity startup Upwind Security for nearly $4 billion, according to someone with direct knowledge of the talks, the latest sign of white-hot interest in such firms. Upwind has fielded other takeover attempts from multiple bidders in recent months but hasn’t accepted any offers. It is finalizing a $300 million funding round at a roughly $3.8 billion valuation, meaning the Datadog offer doesn’t carry much of a premium over the private valuation, said two people with knowledge of the situation. The startup sells software to keep tabs on applications, including so-called AI agents, that run in the cloud and to detect and automatically respond to potential evidence of hacks or breaches.
korean_title: 데이터독, 클라우드 보안 스타트업 '업윈드'에 40억 달러 인수 제안
summary_3_lines: 엔터프라이즈 소프트웨어 기업 데이터독이 이스라엘 클라우드 보안 스타트업 업윈드 시큐리티(Upwind Security)에 약 40억 달러(약 5조 5천억 원) 규모의 인수를 제안했습니다.
업윈드는 클라우드에서 실행되는 AI 에이전트 및 애플리케이션을 모니터링하고 침해 위협을 자동 감지·대응하는 소프트웨어를 제공하며 여러 곳의 인수 러브콜을 받고 있습니다.
현재 업윈드는 38억 달러 기업가치로 3억 달러 규모의 투자 유치를 마무리 중이어서 데이터독의 제안에 큰 프리미엄이 붙지 않아 공식 수락하지 않은 상태입니다.
business_insight: 클라우드 환경 내 AI 에이전트 모니터링과 보안이 핵심 인프라로 급부상하면서, 옵저버빌리티 플랫폼 기업들의 대규모 보안 스타트업 인수 경쟁이 더욱 치열해지고 있습니다.

title: SB Energy Considers Waiting Until December or Later for an IPO
summary: SB Energy, the SoftBank Group–controlled developer of a massive planned Ohio data center project for OpenAI, is considering going public in December or possibly waiting until next year, according to people familiar with the discussions. That is a later timeline than previously expected. The data center developer was aiming to go public as soon as September, The Information reported in August . But since then, the public market has soured on initial public offerings from data center and AI cloud companies. Australian cloud firm Firmus yanked its IPO plans earlier this month, and others are considering delaying their offerings.
korean_title: 소프트뱅크 산하 SB에너지, 시장 침체로 IPO 일정 12월 이후로 연기 검토
summary_3_lines: 소프트뱅크 그룹 산하이자 오하이오주에서 대규모 오픈AI 데이터센터 프로젝트를 개발 중인 SB에너지가 IPO 시점을 12월 또는 내년으로 연기하는 방안을 검토 중입니다.
당초 올해 9월 조기 상장을 목표로 했으나, 최근 데이터센터 및 AI 클라우드 섹터 전반에 대한 공모주 시장의 투자 심리가 냉각되면서 일정 조정이 불가피해졌습니다.
호주 클라우드 기업 퍼머스(Firmus)가 이달 초 IPO 계획을 철회하는 등 관련 인프라 기업들의 상장 지연 움직임이 확산되고 있습니다.
business_insight: AI 인프라 및 데이터센터 관련 기업들의 자금 조달 수요는 여전히 높으나, 수익성 입증에 대한 공모 시장의 눈높이가 엄격해지면서 무리한 조기 상장 대신 시장 회복을 기다리는 전략적 지연이 늘고 있습니다.

title: Utopai Becomes a Unicorn as Video AI Takes Off
summary: While much of the AI industry has fixated on new personal AI assistants from Meta and OpenAI , video AI is enjoying a quiet renaissance. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg is teaming up with the former head of OpenAI’s Sora app to launch a new AI film company . Startup Higgsfield quadrupled its valuation to $5.4 billion in August. And Kling AI , the video unit of Chinese social media giant Kuaishou Technology , raised nearly $3 billion at a $15 billion valuation over the summer. The latest video AI company to seize this moment is Utopai Studios , a 4-year-old film startup based in Mountain View, Calif. Utopai closed a funding round for $60 million that valued it at $1 billion and has already received term sheets for a subsequent round that would value the company at $2 billion to $3 billion, according to someone close to the company. The enthusiasm for video AI startups follows improvements in the quality and length of the clips that video AI models can generate. In September, Higgsfield announced that it had crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue, showing that the technology has serious commercial potential.
korean_title: 비디오 AI 스타트업 유토파이, 10억 달러 가치 인정받으며 유니콘 등극
summary_3_lines: 퍼스널 AI 비서 경쟁 속에서 생성 품질과 영상 길이가 대폭 개선된 비디오 AI 분야가 조용한 르네상스를 맞이하고 있습니다.
미국 캘리포니아 마운틴뷰 기반의 영화 제작 스타트업 유토파이(Utopai Studios)가 6,000만 달러 규모의 투자를 유치하며 기업가치 10억 달러의 유니콘 반열에 올랐습니다.
힉스필드(Higgsfield)의 연환산 매출 10억 달러 돌파와 중국 콰이쇼우의 클링 AI(Kling AI) 대규모 펀딩 등 비디오 AI의 상업적 수익화 잠재력이 시장에서 강력히 입증되고 있습니다.
business_insight: 텍스트·음성 기반 보조 모델에 이어 엔터테인먼트 및 미디어 제작 현장에 직접 투입 가능한 영상 생성 AI가 확실한 수익 지표를 증명하며 차세대 고가치 투자처로 급부상하고 있습니다.
